newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech Sporitelna needs efficient owners - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech Sporitelna needs efficient owners - analysts.

text.p: Shares in Ceska Sporitelna a.s., the largest Czech savings bank, could become attractive if a suitable owner acquires a large minority stake and stresses efficiency, analysts said.
But that may take a while.
The secretive investment group Motoinvest, which says it has a 10-15 percent stake in Sporitelna, has been unsuccessful so far in seeking a buyer for the shares since last summer.

Motoinvest -- which bought shares in Sporitelna, and another bank, Agrobanka a.s. -- has said it would divest its banking sector shares due to the hostility toward it shown by government officials and the central bank.
Officials have frequently said the group was unwelcome because of its opaque financial and ownership structure.
"The Motoinvest case shows how an equity stake has concrete political consequence... there is no seriously interested buyer (for Sporitelna)," Jan Chudomel of Motoinvest told Reuters.
The state holds a 45 percent stake in Sporitelna which gives it strong control as some 15 percent is owned by municipalities which lack voting rights.
Other owners and their exact stakes are unknown.
Analysts have cast doubt on the efficiency of the former communist-era savings bank which now has about 1,800 branches throughout the country, and 19,000 employees.

"If a strong, trustworthy and transparent party, preferably experienced in the banking sector, becomes the new owner (of the Motoinvest stake), it will have a significant positive influence on the value of Sporitelna," said Richard Podpiera of brokerage Atlantik Financial Markets.
"The current ownership structure doesn't create sufficient pressure on the increase of efficiency," Podpiera said.
Josef Kovalovsky, an equities analyst at CSOB, said Sporitelna's management must move to keep its promise to cut a third of its branches, and reduce the bank's payroll.

Sporitelna's management has said it would make deep cuts in staff and its branch network, but the results have yet to be seen. A spokesman told Reuters planned redundancies of 5,000 workers would be carried out over a five-year period.
"A positive impact would of course be expected if there is not a disintegration of this trend (in cuts)," said Kovalovsky.
Sporitelna runs over 2.4 million liquid deposit accounts, according to the bank's own data at the end of 1996.
Clients' deposits, at 290 billion crowns ($10.4 billion) at the end of the third quarter, constitute 80 percent of the bank's resources.
Sporitelna, still the elephant on the interbank market, cut credit exposure to other banks to 20 percent of total assets in the third quarter of 1996 from 32 percent at the end of 1995.
Risky loans to small banks forced the creation of an additional nine billion crowns in reserves in 1995, slashing net profit to just 263 million crowns.
Sporitelna set its 1996 net profit plan at 2.1 billion crowns, but analysts are cautious, pointing out the continuing problems of small Czech banks last year.

"Due to the problems in the banking sector, Ceska Sporitelna will be forced to create larger (than expected) reserves and provisions," said Marcela Gronychova of OFT Brokers. "That makes us believe that the 1996 profit will be lower (than originally forecast)."
Analysts' forecast put 1996 net profit in a range between 1.8 and 2.0 billion crowns.
Sporitelna's shares have fallen from last September's height of 365 crowns to 285 in November, but climbed back to around 325 in the past weeks. The stock closed down five crowns on Monday at 315.
Most analysts recommended it as a buy at up to 340 crowns.
-- Prague Newsrooom, 42-2-2423-0003 ($ = 27.89 Czech Crowns)
